job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Nora Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my twin brothers, who are fifteen, in a terraced house in Pellam. I get up for morning prayers, make breakfast for the boys, and then I'm at the dining-room table for applications. On Tuesdays and Thursdays I keep the books for our church's food pantry, unpaid, which keeps my hands busy. In the evening I help my brothers with homework and cook dinner when my mother works late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what did you do in your internships?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied accounting and finance, finishing top of my year. I did an audit internship at a firm called Whitlock Ames, mostly testing samples of invoices, and a second one in the finance office of a hospital trust. The hospital taught me that every number is a ward or a nurse or a bed. I came away wanting a steady job where I can look after people's money honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, which we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reassuring, but I'd add that nothing replaces care and honesty. A tool might sort invoices faster, but it doesn't know when the numbers are wrong because someone is struggling. I'd say that to my friends at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be anxious about my own situation. I've been applying for months, I have a student loan, and about two months saved. The world staying the same doesn't give me an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, especially to firms that are part of the community, like the local accountancy practice and the hospital trust. I'd go back to Whitlock Ames and ask for a chat with the manager. I'd also keep the food pantry books, because they might lead to a reference, and I enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than frightened. I trust it will work out, but trust and worry can sit side by side. When it's heavy, I pray and then I cook, and it passes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the pantry work teach you that your degree didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That money is about people. At the pantry I count tins and donations, and when the numbers are short I know who went without. A degree teaches you how to record a loss, but the pantry taught me what it means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a job offer came from far away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it carefully and pray on it. I'd not want to leave my brothers at an important age, and my mother depends on me a lot. But if the job was good and the move short, a couple of hours away, I'd go and come home on weekends.

say: I'd say nothing replaces **care and honesty**, and a tool doesn't know why numbers are wrong.
I'd say it to my friends at **church**.
think: I'm still anxious about my situation: **months** of applying, a loan and two months saved.
The world staying the same doesn't give me an **offer**.
do: Apply to **community-minded** firms like the local accountancy practice and the hospital trust.
Ask the manager at **Whitlock Ames** for a chat.
Keep the **food pantry** books for the reference.
feel: **Uneasy** more than frightened, steadied by prayer and cooking.
S0.quote: At the pantry I count tins and donations, and when the numbers are short I know who went without.
fieldNote: Nora's calm is **faith-based**, but she is clear that her money worry is real.
The pantry books give her meaning and a possible reference.
She would move for a good job only if it's near enough to come home at weekends, which reflects her family role.

steps.text: Apply to the local accountancy practice and the hospital trust
Ask the manager at Whitlock Ames for a meeting
Keep doing the food pantry books for a reference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should welcome what helps but not lose people in the process. I'd tell friends that employers should keep training young people. And I'd say churches and clubs can help people retrain, like adult classes in the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I see the audit work I did going first. Sampling invoices, matching them, writing the first notes, that was my internship. I'd be worried my kind of first job gets fewer, and I'd be competing with a lot of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a colleague I trust to show me the tools, and then learn them for real, not just try them once. I'd keep my spending down, put aside a fixed amount from the little I earn, and apply widely, including to the hospital trust. I'd also ask my pastor if anyone in the congregation works at a firm that takes graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not paralysed. It's like seeing clouds and knowing you need to bring a coat. I don't enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you feel the change first, in the jobs you apply for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whitlock Ames had ten people in the audit team, and I could see that half the work could be done by a program. The partners are good people, and I think they'd try to keep staff, but they have to compete. I'd worry about the temporary staff first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your community would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Okonkwo, who is fifty-five and does the books at a local garage. He's honest, and he's good, but he's never moved from paper. If the garage drops him, there's not much for him locally. I'd want us as a church to see him right.

say: I'd say we should welcome what helps but **not lose people** in the process.
I'd say churches can offer **retraining classes** in the hall.
think: The audit work I did, sampling and matching invoices, is **going first**.
I'm worried my kind of **first job** gets scarcer.
do: Ask a colleague I trust to show me the **tools** properly.
Put aside a **fixed amount** monthly and keep spending low.
Ask my **pastor** whether anyone in the congregation works at a graduate firm.
feel: **Anxious but not paralysed**, like seeing clouds and bringing a coat.
S1.quote: Whitlock Ames had ten people in the audit team, and I could see that half the work could be done by a program.
fieldNote: Nora sees **specific tasks** at risk and names a real neighbour, Mr Okonkwo, as someone who might be hurt.
Her routes for help are community-based: pastor, congregation, church hall classes.
Learning the tools is conditional on a trusted colleague, reflecting her steady profile.

steps.text: Ask a trusted colleague to show me the tools properly
Put aside a fixed amount from every payment
Ask my pastor for contacts at firms that take graduates
Apply to the hospital trust finance office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should stay together and look after each other. I'd say this is a time for families and churches to step up, and for government to help those who can't. I'd ask people to check on their neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be afraid. Most of what I learned is thinking work, and in two years there's no time to find a different footing. I'd worry about my father, a pharmacist who might be fine, and my brothers, who are about to choose subjects at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any honest job, even in a shop or the pantry's logistics team, to bring money in. I'd save everything I could and stop all spending that isn't food, rent share and the phone. And I'd help my brothers think about trades and skills with people in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, truly. I'd feel my heart beat faster, and then I'd go to my room and pray, and then I'd come out and cook dinner as normal. That's how I'd get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents and brothers that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them calmly that things may change quickly, and that I have a plan. My father would hold my hand, my mother would worry, and the boys would ask if they still have to study. I'd say yes, but we'll choose carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you stop doing first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: New clothes, any trip, and the small gifts I give at church. I'd keep the tithe, because that's a promise, and the food I cook for the pantry. Everything else goes.

say: I'd say we should **stay together** and look after each other.
I'd ask people to **check on their neighbours**.
think: I'd be **afraid**, because there is no time to find a different footing.
I'd worry about my **brothers**, who are about to choose their school subjects.
do: Take **any honest job**, even in a shop, to bring money in.
Save everything and stop spending except **essentials**: food, rent share and phone.
Help my brothers think about **trades** and work with people in it.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a racing heart, then prayer and cooking dinner as normal.
S2.quote: I'd feel my heart beat faster, and then I'd go to my room and pray, and then I'd come out and cook dinner as normal.
fieldNote: Nora's response is **ritualised**: fear, prayer, then normal duties.
Her worry spreads to her brothers' subject choices, a clear family-plans angle.
She would protect the tithe and the pantry cooking even in crisis, which shows her priorities.

steps.text: Take any honest job, even in a shop, to bring money in
Stop all spending except food, rent share and phone
Lean on my parents and church for meals and support
Help my brothers choose subjects that lead to trades with people in them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time to prepare if we start together. I'd say employers should keep young people on and not just hire the cheapest tools. I'd tell the boys' school that they should teach people skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious but hopeful. I could find a first job, learn what the tools do, and make myself someone people trust with money. That trust is what I'd count on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job at a firm that does careful work, like a local practice, and learn the tools there. I'd qualify as an accountant, since a signature will still matter. And I'd save a third of my pay, and help my brothers choose their futures with some thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but like a long hill and not a cliff. I can see the top, and I can pace myself. I'd keep praying about it, but not only that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years change what you do for your brothers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brothers will be twenty when the robots arrive. I could help them choose work that has people in it, like nursing or building. I might even pay for a course out of my wages. That feels like a good use of the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Classes in the church hall, a jobs board, people who'll introduce you to employers. And a place to be honest about being scared, without it being a thing.

I'd say employers should **keep young people on**, not only buy cheap tools.

That trust is what I'd **count on**.

feel: **Anxious**, like a long hill and not a cliff, with a top I can see.

fieldNote: Nora uses the extra years for **others**: her brothers' choices and a contribution from her wages.

steps.text: Take a job at a careful local practice and learn the tools there

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's time to do it kindly, with training, apprenticeships and communities involved. I'd say we shouldn't leave it to a few firms to decide. And I'd say hard work should still count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel mostly at peace. I could build a career, marry, maybe have a child, and help my brothers settle. But I'd still keep a little worry, because ten years goes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job, qualify, and save for a house. I'd learn the tools slowly, as they prove themselves. I'd also take on more at church, like being the treasurer, so I'm known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quiet calm, with some nerves. It's the one where I could see myself at forty, in a house with a garden, and I'd like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The usual things: a quiet life, family close by, honest work. I'd hate to see my community split between those who coped and those who didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you most afraid of losing in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the changes would split people. Some would own the tools and some would be shut out. I'd want my community to have a share, like a training hall or a co-op.

I'd say hard work should still **count**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because two years is not enough for families or churches to prepare, and the people with the least are hurt first. What would help is community: employers who keep faith with their staff, neighbours helping neighbours, and some support that doesn't make people feel small.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of hard work or of learning. I'd like to be given a chance to show it, and I'd like those who gain from these tools to remember who made them possible, the people who did the work before.

headlineQuote: The hospital taught me that every number is a ward or a nurse or a bed.
portrait: **Nora** is a 23-year-old accounting graduate, top of her class, living with her parents and her twin brothers.
She is **traditional**, faith-led and family-minded, and uses AI tools now and then once a colleague has shown they work.
She keeps the books for a church **food pantry** and wants steady, honest work in finance.
She responds with **steady steps**: save, learn what is proven, lean on community, and help her brothers' plans.
Her mood rises to alarmed in the 2-year world and eases to uneasy with a decade.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**, because two years isn't enough for families or churches to prepare, and the poorest are hurt first.
whatWouldHelp: **Community support** and employers who keep faith with staff.
Help that doesn't make people feel small, such as **apprenticeships** and neighbours helping neighbours.
